# Introduction

During the early phase of an outbreak, the most readily observable population-level signal is simply how the number of newly reported cases changes over time. While the speed at which these cases multiply tells us how rapidly the outbreak is expanding, this observed growth rate alone cannot uniquely determine the true transmissibility of the pathogen.

This is because epidemic growth reflects two distinct aspects of transmission. The first is the **magnitude of transmission**, commonly quantified by the reproduction number, $R$: the average number of secondary infections generated by an infected individual. At the beginning of an outbreak in a fully susceptible population, this quantity is referred to as the basic reproduction number, $R_0$. The second is the **timescale of transmission**, described by the generation time: the time between infection in a primary case (the infector) and infection in the corresponding secondary case (the infectee).

These two quantities jointly determine how quickly case numbers grow. For example, the same observed epidemic growth rate could arise from a pathogen that generates relatively many secondary infections over a longer generation time, or from one that generates fewer secondary infections but transmits them more rapidly. Consequently, translating epidemic growth into estimates of the reproduction number requires information about the timing of transmission.

In practice, however, the exact times at which individuals become infected are rarely observed. Generation times are therefore generally not directly measurable. Symptom-onset times are much more readily recorded, making the **serial interval (SI)** a practical observable proxy. The SI is defined as the time between symptom onset in a primary case (the infector) and symptom onset in the corresponding secondary case (the infectee). Although the SI is not identical to the generation time, it is commonly used to inform the transmission-timescale distribution required to estimate reproduction numbers from epidemic growth [@fine2003; @ganyani2020]. Accurate estimation of the SI is therefore important for quantifying disease transmissibility.

![Generation time and serial interval for one infector--infectee pair. The horizontal arrows show time rather than a scaled numerical axis; the upper and lower timelines represent the infector and infectee. Teal markers denote infection and orange markers denote symptom onset. The teal span measures infection-to-infection generation time, whereas the orange span measures onset-to-onset serial interval.](<../../../../meeting_summarys/report/plot/plot for gernation time and serial interval.png>){#fig-generation-serial width="90%"}

Despite its epidemiological importance, the SI is often difficult to measure directly in real outbreak settings. Surveillance data commonly record symptom-onset dates, but the transmission links connecting individual cases are typically unobserved. In other words, researchers may know when each case developed symptoms without knowing exactly who infected whom. As illustrated in panel A of @fig-unobserved-pathways, several different transmission networks may therefore be compatible with the same observed onset data.

![Why onset dates alone do not identify transmission links. Panel A orders cases from earlier to later symptom onset along a schematic time axis; dotted arrows mark possible but unobserved infector--infectee links. Panel B measures the ICC interval from the index case to Case 3 and contrasts direct, intermediate-case, and common-source pathways that could produce it. There is no numerical vertical axis.](<../../../../meeting_summarys/report/plot/plot for unobserved infection pairs .png>){#fig-unobserved-pathways width="90%"}

In household or small-cluster settings, the underlying transmission network is typically unobserved. However, one well-defined quantity can still be constructed directly from the available symptom-onset data: the index case-to-case (ICC) interval. By identifying the first recognised symptomatic individual as the index case, the ICC interval for each subsequent case is defined as the elapsed time between that case's symptom onset and the symptom onset of the index case. For a non-index case $i$, let $S_i$ be that case's symptom-onset time and $S_0$ the index case's symptom-onset time. The underlying continuous ICC interval is

$$
C_i=S_i-S_0.
$$

Here, $C_i$ is the continuous ICC interval for non-index case $i$; $S_i$ and $S_0$ are the symptom-onset times of case $i$ and the index case, respectively.


Because the index case is selected as the first symptomatic case, an ICC interval is non-negative. This differs from a direct SI, which can be negative when the infectee develops symptoms before the infector. Importantly, calculating an ICC interval requires only observed symptom-onset times and does not require the underlying infector--infectee pair to be known. It therefore provides a practical way to summarise the timing information available from household or small-cluster outbreak data.

![Construction of index case-to-case (ICC) intervals. The horizontal timeline orders symptom onsets; each arrow starts at the index case's onset and ends at a later case's onset. The three arrows illustrate that a separate ICC interval is observed for each subsequent case without identifying who infected whom. This is a schematic, so neither axis has a numerical scale.](<../../../../meeting_summarys/presentation/semester2/ICC interval(2).png>){#fig-icc-interval-example width="90%"}


However, an ICC interval is not necessarily a direct serial interval. The ICC is defined relative to the index case, whereas the SI is defined specifically between a true infector and their infectee. Because the underlying transmission chain is unobserved, the same ICC interval may be compatible with several different transmission pathways, including direct transmission, transmission through intermediate cases, or infection from a common source, as illustrated in panel B of @fig-unobserved-pathways. Each pathway implies a different relationship between the ICC interval and the underlying SI.

Consequently, symptom-onset data alone cannot determine which transmission pathway generated a particular ICC observation. Estimating the underlying SI distribution requires a statistical framework that accounts for uncertainty in these latent transmission pathways. The following section introduces the mixture-model framework proposed by Vink et al. (2014) to address this problem.
