: Comparison of estimated serial interval means and standard deviations (days) between the Normal and Lognormal models across four scabies outbreak datasets. {#tbl-scabies-comparison}


@fig-scabies-model-overlay compares the fitted Normal and Lognormal ICC mixture distributions across the four scabies datasets, while @tbl-scabies-comparison presents the corresponding SI parameter estimates. Overall, the two models produced broadly comparable estimates, with the Lognormal model yielding slightly higher SI means in three datasets and an identical mean in the remaining dataset. This tendency may reflect the right-skewed shape of the Lognormal distribution, which allows the underlying PS component to accommodate a longer right tail. Consequently, some longer ICC intervals may be explained differently under the two distributional assumptions, potentially contributing to the slightly higher SI mean estimates. However, this interpretation remains tentative, as the fitted mixture curves do not directly reveal the posterior pathway assignments.

For the Akunzirwe et al. dataset (Panel A of @fig-scabies-model-overlay), the ICC intervals were relatively widely dispersed, and the two fitted curves showed more noticeable differences than in the other datasets. As reported in @tbl-scabies-comparison, the estimated SI mean increased from 122.9 days under the Normal assumption to 125.4 days under the Lognormal assumption, while the SD increased more substantially from 26.9 to 31.0 days. The Lognormal mixture exhibited a slightly broader main peak and a lower fitted density than the Normal mixture at shorter ICC intervals, where the CP component is expected to contribute. These differences suggest that the two models may represent the shorter intervals and the main concentration of observations differently. The larger Lognormal SD may partly reflect this difference in the fitted mixture structure, although the relative contributions of individual pathways cannot be determined from the overall curves alone.

For the Ariza et al. dataset (Panel B of @fig-scabies-model-overlay), the ICC intervals were strongly concentrated around 90–105 days, and the fitted Normal and Lognormal curves closely overlapped around the main peak. Both models estimated an identical SI mean of 98.4 days, with only a small increase in SD from 8.5 to 9.0 days under the Lognormal assumption (@tbl-scabies-comparison). Similarly, in the Kaburi et al. dataset (Panel C of @fig-scabies-model-overlay), both models captured the pronounced concentration of ICC intervals around 160–175 days. The estimated SI means were nearly identical (167.3 and 167.4 days), while the SD increased slightly from 9.7 to 10.7 days (@tbl-scabies-comparison). These results indicate that changing the SI distributional assumption had relatively little influence on parameter estimates in these two datasets.

For the Tjon-Kon-Fat et al. dataset (Panel D of @fig-scabies-model-overlay), the fitted Normal and Lognormal mixture curves were also very similar across the ICC range. As reported in @tbl-scabies-comparison, the estimated SI mean increased slightly from 110.7 to 112.3 days under the Lognormal assumption, whereas the estimated SD decreased from 16.1 to 15.2 days. Unlike the other three datasets, the Lognormal model therefore produced a marginally smaller estimate of SI variability, although the overall differences remained modest.

Taken together, @fig-scabies-model-overlay and @tbl-scabies-comparison demonstrate that the Lognormal extension can produce SI parameter estimates broadly consistent with those obtained under the established Normal model. Despite some differences in the fitted mixture shapes, particularly in the Akunzirwe dataset, the two models generally provided similar representations of the ICC timing patterns. This agreement provides additional support for the practical feasibility of the Lognormal extension and increases confidence in its application to real outbreak data. Nevertheless, because the true SI distributions are unknown, these findings do not establish that the Lognormal assumption provides more accurate estimates or a superior fit. Rather, the extension offers an additional distributional option for analysing diseases whose underlying serial intervals may be positive and right-skewed.



# Software Implementation

## Package context and purpose

The proposed Lognormal extension was implemented within the existing `{mitey}` R package, originally developed to support serial-interval estimation and reproduction-number analysis using infectious-disease outbreak data. The package has two main functions: estimating the mean and standard deviation of the serial interval (SI) from index-case-to-case (ICC) intervals using the transmission-pathway framework of Vink et al., and estimating the time-varying reproduction number using the Wallinga–Lipsitch method. This project focuses exclusively on extending the SI estimation component, leaving the reproduction-number functionality unchanged.

The original `si_estim()` function supports Normal and Gamma assumptions for the underlying SI distribution. This project introduces a Lognormal option to accommodate right-skewed SI distributions. Rather than replacing the existing models, the extension provides greater flexibility in selecting an appropriate distributional assumption while preserving the original workflow of fitting ICC intervals and estimating SI parameters and transmission-pathway proportions.

## Input layer: adding the Lognormal option

The primary user-facing modification is the addition of `dist = "lognormal"` to `si_estim()`, alongside the existing `"normal"` and `"gamma"` options. The input remains a numeric vector of ICC intervals measured in days. Negative intervals are not permitted under the Lognormal specification, while zero-day observations are retained to account for cases with symptom onset recorded on the same day.

The existing estimation controls, including the maximum number of EM iterations, initial SI mean and standard deviation, convergence tolerance, and multiple starting values, remain available. Thus, all three distributional assumptions can be fitted through the same function interface.

## Mixture-model layer: pathway-specific densities

Introducing the Lognormal assumption required modifications to the four pathway-specific density functions. The primary-secondary (PS) component follows the underlying Lognormal SI distribution exactly, while the co-primary (CP) component is represented by a Half-Normal working approximation. The primary-tertiary (PT) and primary-quaternary (PQ) components involve sums of two and three independent Lognormal variables, respectively. Since these sums lack convenient closed-form densities, Fenton–Wilkinson Lognormal approximations were introduced to match their natural-scale means and variances.

These component densities were incorporated into the mixture likelihood and the functions used to evaluate discrete ICC observations. Because symptom-onset dates are recorded in calendar days, the component densities are numerically integrated over the corresponding daily observation intervals. This preserves the original discretisation framework while accommodating the new distributional assumption.

## Estimation layer: adapting the EM algorithm

The expectation–maximization (EM) procedure was adapted to improve pathway assignment, numerical stability, and convergence assessment.

First, the E-step was modified to calculate posterior responsibilities using the current mixture weights. A responsibility represents the estimated probability that an individual ICC observation belongs to a particular latent transmission pathway. Unlike the previous implementation, which normalised pathway-specific probabilities without accounting for their relative prevalence, the updated calculation uses the weighted sum of probabilities across all four pathways in the denominator. This ensures that the responsibilities reflect both the compatibility of each observation with a pathway and its estimated prevalence in the mixture. The resulting responsibilities are averaged to update the pathway weights, while the underlying Lognormal SI parameters are updated using PS-weighted log-scale moments, subsequently transformed back to the natural scale.

Second, an E/M-decoupled strategy was introduced to accommodate zero-day ICC observations, which occur when two cases have symptom onset recorded on the same day. These observations retain their original zero-day values when calculating discretised probabilities and posterior responsibilities in the E-step. However, because the M-step requires logarithmic transformations, zero values are replaced by a value of one only during the log-scale parameter update. This avoids the undefined $\log(0)$ and prevents extreme negative log values from distorting the estimated SI parameters, particularly the variance, while preserving the original observations for pathway assignment.

Finally, the convergence criterion was strengthened to account for changes in both SI parameters and pathway weights. Previously, convergence was assessed based on changes in the estimated SI mean and standard deviation between successive iterations. The updated procedure additionally requires the maximum absolute change across the four pathway weights to fall below a specified tolerance. Convergence is therefore declared only when the relative changes in the SI mean and standard deviation, together with the absolute changes in pathway weights, satisfy the convergence criterion. This reduces the risk of premature termination when SI parameter estimates appear stable but the underlying pathway allocations are still changing.

## Output layer

The extended implementation preserves the existing output structure. The fitted object returns the estimated natural-scale SI mean and standard deviation, the four pathway weights, convergence status, number of iterations, fitted log-likelihood, and iteration history.

The plotting functions were also extended to support the Lognormal option, allowing the fitted mixture density and its pathway-specific components to be visualised against the ICC distribution. These modifications maintain consistency with the original package while supporting additional distributional assumptions.

## Use in simulation and empirical analysis

The extended implementation was evaluated through simulation studies combining three SI dispersion levels, three transmission-pathway configurations, and four sample sizes. The simulation results were used to assess parameter recovery using RMSE, together with algorithmic convergence and sensitivity to initialization.

The method was subsequently applied to four historical scabies datasets previously analysed using the Normal SI model. The empirical analysis compared estimated SI parameters and fitted mixture densities under the Normal and Lognormal assumptions. As the true SI distributions are unknown, this comparison provides a practical assessment of numerical performance and epidemiological plausibility rather than direct evidence of parameter-recovery accuracy.


# Discussion

This study extended the transmission-pathway mixture framework of Vink et al. [@vink2014] by introducing a Lognormal assumption for the underlying serial interval (SI) distribution. While the original framework and subsequent implementations primarily considered Normal and Gamma distributions, the proposed extension provides an additional option for infectious diseases with long-tailed and right-skewed serial intervals. The extension was implemented within the `{mitey}` R package and evaluated through simulation studies covering different SI dispersion levels, household and small-outbreak transmission structures, and sample sizes, followed by applications to four historical scabies datasets. Overall, the findings demonstrate the feasibility of the Lognormal extension while highlighting the epidemiological conditions under which reliable SI parameter recovery may be achieved.

The simulation results in @tbl-main-simulation and @fig-main-simulation-summary suggest that the proposed method is most promising for infectious diseases with relatively low or moderate SI dispersion, particularly in household or small-population outbreaks where primary-secondary (PS) transmission contributes a substantial proportion of the ICC intervals. Under the low-dispersion baseline scenario, where PS observations accounted for 50% of the mixture, the method achieved RMSE values of 0.66 and 0.43 days for the SI mean and standard deviation, respectively, with 100% convergence. However, estimation accuracy deteriorated considerably when the PS proportion decreased and other pathways became more dominant, even under the same low-dispersion setting. Under moderate dispersion, the converged estimates generally showed relatively low RMSE, although many runs did not satisfy the convergence criterion within 300 iterations, suggesting that more iterations may be required in some cases. In contrast, the high-dispersion scenarios exhibited larger estimation errors and substantial overlap between pathway components. These findings indicate that the applicability of the method depends not only on the SI characteristics of the infectious disease but also on whether the transmission structure of the observed outbreak provides sufficient direct PS information.

Another finding is the sensitivity of parameter recovery to the choice of initial values, as shown in @fig-em-trajectory and @fig-init-sensitivity. The low-dispersion simulations revealed that the algorithm could satisfy its numerical convergence criterion while producing estimates substantially different from the true SI parameters. Further investigation showed that initializing the SI parameters using the empirical mean and standard deviation of the entire ICC dataset could be problematic, particularly when the variability of the ICC mixture substantially exceeded that of the underlying SI distribution. The subsequent sensitivity analysis demonstrated that alternative starting values could substantially improve parameter recovery in some of these scenarios, with the effects depending on the transmission-pathway composition. This highlights the importance of selecting epidemiologically plausible initial parameters rather than relying exclusively on ICC sample moments. Previous applications of the Vink framework have also recognised the importance of initialization. In practical applications, researchers may draw on previous studies or disease-specific epidemiological knowledge to select reasonable starting values, potentially considering multiple initializations to assess the stability of the resulting estimates.

Finally, the application to four historical scabies datasets, summarised in @fig-scabies-model-overlay and @tbl-scabies-comparison, provided an empirical assessment of the Lognormal extension. Across the datasets, the estimated SI means and standard deviations were broadly comparable to those obtained under the original Normal assumption, although some differences were observed in the fitted mixture densities. These findings suggest that the Lognormal extension can produce epidemiologically plausible estimates when applied to real outbreak data, supporting its practical applicability beyond simulated settings. However, because the true SI distributions and transmission links are unknown, this agreement does not establish that the Lognormal assumption provides more accurate estimates or a better fit than the Normal model. Rather, the extension offers an additional distributional option whose suitability should be assessed in relation to the characteristics of the disease and the available outbreak data.

## Limitations

Despite demonstrating the feasibility of the Lognormal extension, the proposed method has several limitations that may affect the accuracy of SI parameter estimation and its applicability to different infectious diseases and outbreak settings.

### Restricted transmission-pathway structure

The proposed method retains the four transmission pathways considered in the original Vink framework: co-primary (CP), primary-secondary (PS), primary-tertiary (PT), and primary-quaternary (PQ). While this structure provides a reasonable representation of transmission in households or small outbreak clusters, real-world outbreaks may involve more complex transmission networks, including additional transmission generations and multiple external introductions.

When the true transmission structure extends beyond these four pathways, some ICC intervals may not be adequately represented by the assumed mixture model. Consequently, the model may incorrectly attribute these observations to the existing components, potentially affecting the estimated pathway proportions and underlying SI parameters. The applicability of the method therefore depends on whether the four-pathway framework adequately represents the transmission structure of the outbreak being studied.

### Pathway overlap, initialization, and practical identifiability

A key limitation of the proposed method is its reliance on the posterior responsibilities assigned to the latent transmission pathways during the E-step. Since the underlying SI parameters are updated using information weighted by the primary-secondary (PS) responsibilities, difficulties in distinguishing transmission pathways may affect subsequent parameter updates and lead to inaccurate SI estimates. However, such difficulties can arise for different reasons, with important implications for whether they can be overcome.

The first concerns the inherent overlap between pathway-specific distributions. For infectious diseases with relatively high SI dispersion, the four transmission-pathway components may overlap substantially even when the true SI parameters are used. Under these conditions, the ICC intervals may provide insufficient information to distinguish the contributions of different pathways, weakening the practical identifiability of the underlying SI parameters. This represents a fundamental challenge to the applicability of the method for highly dispersed SI distributions, which cannot necessarily be resolved by selecting better initial values or allowing more EM iterations.

The second concerns sensitivity to initialization. Even when the true pathway distributions are relatively well separated, unsuitable initial SI parameters may produce fitted component distributions with substantial overlap, leading to inaccurate pathway responsibilities during the E-step. These responsibilities may then influence subsequent parameter updates, causing the algorithm to converge to stable but inaccurate estimates. Unlike the inherent overlap associated with high SI dispersion, this difficulty may be mitigated through more appropriate initialization. As demonstrated by the sensitivity analysis, alternative starting values substantially improved parameter recovery in some of the problematic low-dispersion scenarios.

Therefore, it is important to distinguish between difficulties arising from limited information in the underlying ICC mixture and those introduced by unsuitable initial parameter values. While improved initialization may enhance estimation performance in otherwise favourable settings, it cannot guarantee reliable parameter recovery when the transmission pathways are inherently difficult to distinguish.

### Distributional and observational assumptions

The proposed extension assumes that the underlying SI follows a Lognormal distribution, which is strictly positive and right-skewed. Unlike the Normal distribution, which is symmetric and allows negative SI values, the Lognormal model is therefore intended for infectious diseases whose serial intervals are expected to be positive and exhibit a relatively long right tail. This assumption may be inappropriate for diseases where negative serial intervals occur or where the underlying SI distribution has a substantially different shape.

The framework also assumes that individual serial intervals are independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) and that the ICC intervals are statistically independent. In reality, SI characteristics may vary across individuals due to factors such as age, individual susceptibility, disease progression, or public health interventions. ICC observations from the same household may also be correlated because they share a common index case and transmission environment. However, such individual-level and transmission-related information is not always available in routine surveillance data. The i.i.d. assumption therefore provides a practical simplification, although unaccounted heterogeneity and dependence may affect parameter estimation.

Finally, the discretisation model assumes that the exact symptom-onset time is uniformly distributed within each reported calendar day. In practice, reported onset dates may also be affected by recall errors, inaccurate recording, or other measurement errors. These departures from the assumed observation process may introduce additional uncertainty or bias into the estimated SI distribution.

## Future work

Several directions could further improve the flexibility and applicability of the proposed framework.

First, future research could extend the underlying SI distributional assumptions beyond the existing Normal, Gamma, and Lognormal options. As the shape and variability of serial intervals may differ across infectious diseases, no single distribution is expected to adequately represent all epidemiological settings. Exploring additional distribution families, such as Weibull or generalised Gamma distributions, could broaden the applicability of the framework to diseases with different SI characteristics.

Second, future work should develop systematic criteria to help researchers select an appropriate SI distribution for a given outbreak dataset. Although the `{mitey}` package now supports multiple distributional assumptions, determining which model best represents the underlying SI remains challenging because the true transmission links and SI distribution are generally unknown. Potential approaches include evaluating goodness-of-fit methods, such as smooth tests, alongside methods for comparing candidate models based on their fitted ICC mixture distributions. Such criteria could provide more objective guidance for distribution selection, rather than relying solely on prior assumptions or visual comparisons of fitted curves.

Finally, the transmission-pathway framework could be extended to accommodate more complex outbreak structures, including transmission chains beyond the current four-pathway specification. An important challenge is that long ICC intervals may result either from a long-tailed underlying SI distribution or from transmission through additional generations. If the model does not adequately represent the true transmission structure, it may incorrectly attribute longer ICC intervals to the SI distribution, potentially biasing parameter estimates. Future research should therefore investigate how to determine when additional transmission pathways are epidemiologically warranted and how to incorporate them while maintaining model identifiability. Information about household or outbreak-cluster structure may provide useful guidance for assessing the plausibility of longer transmission chains.


# Appendix

## Appendix A. Additional Details of the EM Estimation Procedure

This appendix provides the mathematical updates and numerical details underlying the EM procedure described in the Methods section. The four transmission pathways, their Log-Normal working densities, and the triangular discretisation of ICC intervals are defined in the main text and are not repeated here. The additional details concern latent pathway responsibilities, PS-weighted parameter updates, zero-day observations, and convergence assessment.

### A.1 Latent Pathway Responsibilities and the Vink Updating Principle

Throughout this Appendix, $N$ is the number of ICC observations, $i\in\{1,\ldots,N\}$ indexes observations, $g$ and $h$ index pathways in $\mathcal G$, and $r=0,1,2,\ldots$ indexes EM iterations. The vector $\mathbf w=(w_g:g\in\mathcal G)$ contains the four pathway weights.

Let $T_i=t_i$ denote the observed integer-day ICC interval for observation $i$, and let $Z_i\in\mathcal G=\{\mathrm{CP},\mathrm{PS},\mathrm{PT},\mathrm{PQ}\}$ denote its unobserved transmission pathway. Define the latent indicator $z_{ig}$, which records whether observation $i$ belongs to pathway $g$:

$$
z_{ig}=\begin{cases}
1,&Z_i=g,\\
0,&Z_i\neq g.
\end{cases}
$$

If the pathway labels were observed, the complete-data log-likelihood associated with pathway membership would be

$$
\ell_c(m,s,\mathbf w)
=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{g\in\mathcal G}
z_{ig}\left\{\log w_g+\log p_{ig}(m,s)\right\},
$$

where $\ell_c$ denotes the complete-data log-likelihood, the subscript $c$ denotes “complete data”, $m$ and $s$ denote the natural-scale SI mean and SD, $w_g$ is the mixture weight of pathway $g$, and $p_{ig}(m,s)$ is the discretised probability of observation $i$ under pathway $g$. The logarithm is the natural logarithm, and the two summation signs combine contributions over all observations and pathways.

At iteration $r$, the E-step replaces the unobserved indicators with the posterior responsibilities $\tau_{ig}^{(r)}$, the conditional probability that pathway $g$ generated observation $i$ under the current parameter values:

$$
\tau_{ig}^{(r)}
=\operatorname{Pr}(Z_i=g\mid T_i=t_i,\mathbf w^{(r)},m^{(r)},s^{(r)})
=\frac{w_g^{(r)}p_{ig}(m^{(r)},s^{(r)})}
{\displaystyle\sum_{h\in\mathcal G}w_h^{(r)}p_{ih}(m^{(r)},s^{(r)})}.
$$

In the denominator, $h$ is a dummy pathway index used to sum over all four possible pathways. The responsibilities satisfy $\sum_g\tau_{ig}^{(r)}=1$ for each observation and provide fractional rather than deterministic pathway assignments. Their average updates the pathway proportions:

$$
w_g^{(r+1)}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\tau_{ig}^{(r)}.
$$

The current weights must enter each E-step because pathway prevalence influences the posterior assignments. Importantly, all four pathways contribute to this weight update, whereas the parameters of the underlying SI distribution are updated using the primary-secondary (PS) responsibilities only. In the original Normal version of the Vink procedure [@vink2014], $\mu^{(r+1)}$ and $(\sigma^2)^{(r+1)}$ denote the updated natural-scale SI mean and variance. Their corresponding PS-weighted updates were

$$
\mu^{(r+1)}
=\frac{\sum_i\tau_{i,\mathrm{PS}}^{(r)}t_i}
{\sum_i\tau_{i,\mathrm{PS}}^{(r)}},
\qquad
(\sigma^2)^{(r+1)}
=\frac{\sum_i\tau_{i,\mathrm{PS}}^{(r)}
(t_i-\mu^{(r+1)})^2}
{\sum_i\tau_{i,\mathrm{PS}}^{(r)}}.
$$

In these expressions, each unbounded sum over $i$ runs over all $N$ observations. The expressions are included for comparison: the Log-Normal extension retains the PS-only updating principle but changes the scale on which the SI moments are calculated.

### A.2 PS-Weighted Updates Under the Log-Normal SI Model

For the Log-Normal extension, write $\log X\sim N(\eta,\zeta^2)$ for a direct SI $X$, where $\eta$ and $\zeta^2$ are the mean and variance of the log-transformed SI. Let $a_i^{(r)}=\tau_{i,\mathrm{PS}}^{(r)}$ be observation $i$'s PS responsibility, and define $Y_i=\log T_i^*$ as its zero-safe log interval, where $T_i^*$ is the zero-safe M-step value described below. Set

$$
A_1^{(r)}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}a_i^{(r)},
\qquad
A_2^{(r)}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left(a_i^{(r)}\right)^2.
$$

Thus, $A_1^{(r)}$ is the total PS responsibility at iteration $r$, while $A_2^{(r)}$ is the sum of squared PS responsibilities used in the finite-sample correction.

The responsibility-weighted log-scale mean and variance are updated by

$$
\eta^{(r+1)}
=\frac{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{N}a_i^{(r)}Y_i}
{A_1^{(r)}},
$$

$$
(\zeta^2)^{(r+1)}
=\frac{A_1^{(r)}}{\left(A_1^{(r)}\right)^2-A_2^{(r)}}
\sum_{i=1}^{N}a_i^{(r)}
\left(Y_i-\eta^{(r+1)}\right)^2.
$$

The second expression is the finite-sample-corrected weighted variance used in the implementation; it is distinct from the uncorrected weighted variance commonly used in a likelihood M-step. The estimates are transformed back to the natural scale as follows, where $\exp(\cdot)$ denotes the exponential function:

$$
m^{(r+1)}
=\exp\left(\eta^{(r+1)}+\frac{(\zeta^2)^{(r+1)}}{2}\right),
$$

$$
s^{(r+1)}
=\sqrt{\left\{\exp\big((\zeta^2)^{(r+1)}\big)-1\right\}
\exp\left\{2\eta^{(r+1)}+(\zeta^2)^{(r+1)}\right\}}.
$$

The PS component represents a single direct SI and therefore follows the target Log-Normal distribution without an additional pathway-density approximation. Restricting the parameter updates to observations weighted by their PS responsibilities limits the direct influence of CP observations and longer-generation PT/PQ intervals. These other pathways still affect the estimates indirectly through their contributions to the E-step denominator and the subsequent PS responsibilities. In particular, misallocation of higher-generation observations to PS can influence the SI estimates despite the PS-only update.

Because this implementation uses corrected responsibility-weighted moments of discretised ICC values rather than an exact maximisation of the full interval-censored mixture likelihood, it should be understood as a Vink-style EM updating procedure rather than a guarantee of monotonic improvement in the full observed-data likelihood.

### A.3 Treatment of Zero-Day ICC Intervals

Zero-day ICC intervals represent valid observations in which cases have symptom onset recorded on the same day. However, extending the Vink updating procedure to a Log-Normal SI distribution introduces a numerical difficulty because the M-step operates on logarithmically transformed intervals, for which

$$
\log(0)=-\infty.
$$

A naive approach would be to replace zero with a very small positive value. However, this produces an extremely negative log observation. If the corresponding interval receives non-negligible PS responsibility, it may pull the estimated log-scale mean downward and substantially inflate the log-scale variance. The resulting PS density becomes more dispersed, potentially altering the posterior responsibilities calculated in subsequent E-steps. These changes may, in turn, further distort the parameter updates, creating a positive-feedback mechanism:

$$
\begin{aligned}
T_i=0
&\longrightarrow \text{extreme negative log value}\\
&\longrightarrow \text{inflated log-scale variance}\\
&\longrightarrow \text{overly dispersed PS density}\\
&\longrightarrow \text{distorted PS responsibilities}\\
&\longrightarrow \text{potential further variance inflation}.
\end{aligned}
$$

To avoid this numerical instability, an **E/M-decoupled zero-handling strategy** was implemented. In the E-step, the original zero-day observation is retained when evaluating the pathway-specific discretised likelihood. In the current implementation, its contribution is calculated as

$$
p_g^{\mathrm{impl}}(0;m,s)
=
\int_0^1 2(1-c)f_g(c;m,s)\,dc.
$$

Here, $p_g^{\mathrm{impl}}(0;m,s)$ is the implemented probability assigned to a zero-day observation under pathway $g$, the superscript “impl” distinguishes this implementation-specific expression from the general discretisation formula, $f_g(c;m,s)$ is pathway $g$'s continuous ICC density at $c$, and $m,s$ are the natural-scale SI mean and SD.

Only during the logarithmic M-step is a separate zero-safe working value introduced:

$$
T_i^*=
\begin{cases}
1, & T_i=0,\\
T_i, & T_i>0,
\end{cases}
\qquad
Y_i=\log(T_i^*).
$$

Thus, a zero-day observation contributes $Y_i=0$ to the responsibility-weighted log-scale parameter updates, avoiding the extreme negative log values that could otherwise destabilise estimation. The replacement value of one is a computational proxy rather than an assumption that the underlying continuous ICC interval lasted exactly one day.

This separation retains the observed zero-day interval during pathway classification while preventing the logarithmic singularity from entering the M-step. Although the proxy does not constitute an exact treatment of interval censoring in the parameter update, it provides a numerically stable implementation of the PS-weighted updating procedure.

### A.4 Initialization and Joint Convergence Criterion

The implementation begins with initial natural-scale SI parameters $(m^{(0)},s^{(0)})$ and equal initial pathway weights $w_g^{(0)}=1/4$. Unless alternative starting parameters are supplied, the initial mean and SD are obtained from the empirical ICC intervals. The sensitivity analysis in the Results section examines the effect of varying these initial values while keeping the ICC datasets fixed.

At iteration $r$, the stopping rule monitors relative changes in the natural-scale SI parameters and the largest absolute change in the four mixture weights:

$$
\Delta_m^{(r)}
=\frac{|m^{(r+1)}-m^{(r)}|}{|m^{(r)}|+\epsilon},
\qquad
\Delta_s^{(r)}
=\frac{|s^{(r+1)}-s^{(r)}|}{|s^{(r)}|+\epsilon},
$$

$$
\Delta_w^{(r)}
=\max_{g\in\mathcal G}\left|w_g^{(r+1)}-w_g^{(r)}\right|,
$$

Here, $\Delta_m^{(r)}$ and $\Delta_s^{(r)}$ are the relative changes in the natural-scale SI mean and SD, $\Delta_w^{(r)}$ is the largest absolute change among the four weights, and $\epsilon$ is a small positive constant that prevents division by zero. Numerical convergence is declared only when

$$
\Delta_m^{(r)}<\mathrm{tol},\qquad
\Delta_s^{(r)}<\mathrm{tol},\qquad
\Delta_w^{(r)}<\mathrm{tol}.
$$

The symbol $\mathrm{tol}$ denotes the positive convergence tolerance, whose default value is $10^{-6}$. Joint monitoring prevents termination based only on apparently stable SI parameters while pathway weights are still changing. The simulation analyses imposed a maximum of 300 iterations. Nevertheless, satisfying this stopping rule indicates numerical stability of the updates, not necessarily accurate recovery of the generating SI parameters, as demonstrated by the low-dispersion simulation and initialization sensitivity results.


## Appendix B. Assessment of Component-Density Approximations

The Log-Normal extension uses computationally tractable working densities for the co-primary (CP), primary-tertiary (PT), and primary-quaternary (PQ) transmission pathways. As described in the Methods section, the ideal CP interval is the absolute difference of two independent Log-Normal serial intervals, whereas PT and PQ are sums of two and three independent intervals, respectively. The PS pathway comprises one direct serial interval and is represented exactly.

This appendix evaluates how closely these working densities approximate their ideal continuous distributions. The assessment concerns distributional approximation rather than bias in estimated SI parameters or the additional effects of rounding ICC intervals to calendar days.

### B.1 Co-primary pathway: Half-Normal approximation

Let $X_1$ and $X_2$ denote independent serial intervals following the same Log-Normal distribution with natural-scale mean $m$ and standard deviation $s$. The exact co-primary interval is $C_{\mathrm{CP}}=|X_1-X_2|$. Writing $f_X$ for the density of one SI, its exact continuous density can be expressed as

$$
f_{\mathrm{CP}}^{\mathrm{exact}}(c)
=
2\int_0^\infty f_X(x)f_X(x+c)\,dx,
\qquad c\geq 0.
$$

The working model approximates the signed difference $X_1-X_2$ by a Normal distribution with mean zero and variance $2s^2$, giving the Half-Normal density

$$
f_{\mathrm{CP}}^{\mathrm{HN}}(c)
=
\frac{1}{s\sqrt{\pi}}
\exp\left(-\frac{c^2}{4s^2}\right),
\qquad c\geq 0.
$$

This approximation preserves the variance scale of the signed difference before taking its absolute value, but does not necessarily reproduce the moments or shape of the exact CP distribution. In particular, the exact density depends on both $m$ and $s$, whereas the Half-Normal approximation depends only on $s$. Differences in concentration near zero, curvature, and tail behaviour may therefore arise, especially when the underlying SI distribution is highly dispersed and right-skewed.

### B.2 PT and PQ pathways: Distributional cost of the Fenton--Wilkinson approximation

The Fenton--Wilkinson (FW) approximation replaces a sum of independent Log-Normal serial intervals with a single Log-Normal distribution matching its exact natural-scale mean and variance.

For $S_n=\sum_{j=1}^{n}X_j$, the exact moments are $E(S_n)=nm$ and $\operatorname{Var}(S_n)=ns^2$, where $n=2$ for PT and $n=3$ for PQ. Although the FW approximation preserves these two moments, it does not necessarily reproduce higher-order distributional characteristics, particularly skewness.

Let

$$
c_v=\frac{s}{m}
$$

denote the coefficient of variation of the underlying SI distribution.

The skewness of a single Log-Normal variable is $(c_v^2+3)c_v$. Since the serial intervals are independent, the skewness of their sum is

$$
\gamma_{\mathrm{sum},n}
=
\frac{(c_v^2+3)c_v}{\sqrt{n}}.
$$

The moment-matched FW distribution has coefficient of variation $c_v/\sqrt{n}$. Its skewness is therefore

$$
\gamma_{\mathrm{FW},n}
=
\frac{(c_v^2/n+3)c_v}{\sqrt{n}}.
$$

The resulting skewness difference is

$$
\Delta\gamma_n
=
\gamma_{\mathrm{sum},n}
-
\gamma_{\mathrm{FW},n}
=
\frac{c_v^3(1-1/n)}{\sqrt{n}},
\qquad n>1.
$$

Because $\Delta\gamma_n>0$, the FW approximation has lower overall positive skewness than the exact sum. The discrepancy increases with $c_v^3$, suggesting that the approximation becomes less accurate as the underlying SI distribution becomes more variable and strongly right-skewed.

Importantly, this result concerns the standardised third moment. It does not imply that the FW density is lower than the exact density at every point in the right tail.

### B.3 Numerical assessment of approximation accuracy

To assess the magnitude of these distributional discrepancies, the ideal and working pathway-specific densities were compared under the three SI settings used in the main simulation: low dispersion $(m,s)=(15,3)$, moderate dispersion $(2,2)$, and high dispersion $(5,10)$.

For CP, the exact absolute-difference density was evaluated numerically and compared with its Half-Normal approximation. For PT and PQ, exact sums of independent Log-Normal intervals were evaluated using numerical convolution and compared with their FW approximations.

The accuracy of each approximation was quantified using the density overlap coefficient,

$$
\operatorname{OVL}(f,g)
=
\int_0^\infty
\min\{f(c),g(c)\}\,dc
=
1-\frac{1}{2}
\int_0^\infty |f(c)-g(c)|\,dc.
$$

Values closer to 100% indicate greater agreement between the two continuous densities.

![Comparison of ideal and working pathway-specific ICC densities under three Log-Normal SI dispersion settings. Rows represent low ($m=15$, $s=3$), moderate ($m=2$, $s=2$), and high ($m=5$, $s=10$) dispersion; columns correspond to CP, PS, PT, and PQ pathways. The horizontal axis shows ICC interval (days) and the vertical axis shows density. Solid dark curves represent the ideal continuous distributions, while dashed orange curves represent the working approximations; shaded regions indicate differences between them. CP uses a Half-Normal approximation to the absolute difference of two independent Log-Normal intervals, PS is exact, and PT/PQ use Fenton--Wilkinson approximations. Panel annotations report density overlap percentages calculated over the full numerical domain. Comparisons precede calendar-day discretisation. In the main simulation, CP observations were generated using the Half-Normal working model rather than the exact Log-Normal difference distribution.](../Simulation_results/component_approximation_comparison_corrected.png){#fig-component-approximation width="100%"}

As shown in @fig-component-approximation, the working densities closely approximate their ideal counterparts under low SI dispersion. The density overlaps are approximately 98.24% for CP, 99.97% for PT, and 99.96% for PQ, while the PS component is represented exactly.

As shown in @fig-component-approximation, the discrepancies become more pronounced as dispersion increases. Under moderate dispersion, CP overlap decreases to approximately 77.51%, compared with 98.42% and 97.99% for PT and PQ. Under high dispersion, CP overlap decreases further to approximately 58.81%, whereas PT and PQ retain overlaps of approximately 95.88% and 94.40%, respectively.

The numerical comparisons in @fig-component-approximation are consistent with the theoretical expectations. The increasingly large FW skewness gap is reflected in declining density overlap under higher dispersion, although the overall PT/PQ approximations remain relatively close. In contrast, the Half-Normal approximation can differ substantially from the exact CP density, particularly near zero.

The results in @fig-component-approximation indicate that approximation accuracy depends on the underlying SI dispersion and transmission pathway. However, density overlap does not directly quantify bias in EM-based SI estimation. The effect of approximation error on estimated parameters also depends on pathway weights, discretised likelihood contributions, and posterior pathway responsibilities.

Furthermore, because the main simulation generated CP observations using the Half-Normal working model, it did not separately assess the additional parameter-estimation error that might arise when real CP intervals follow the exact absolute difference of independent Log-Normal serial intervals.


## Supplementary simulation results

The following figures provide the complete simulation summaries for sample sizes other than the $N=100$ reference setting. Each figure displays the distribution of parameter-estimation bias for converged runs and the convergence rate over all 100 repetitions. The iteration cap is 300. The RMSE summaries for all 36 simulation configurations are given in @tbl-all-simulation-results.

#| label: fig-simulation-n20

Rows show low, moderate, and high SI dispersion; the horizontal categories are baseline, CP-heavy, and higher-generation-heavy pathway profiles. Left and middle panels show estimated minus true SI mean and SD (days) for converged runs: coloured dots are repetitions, black points are mean biases with 5th--95th percentile ranges, and red dashed lines mark zero. Right panels show convergence percentage across all 100 repetitions, with profile vertically and percentage horizontally. Compare recovery and convergence under the 300-iteration cap."
